claim: Endogenous DVL2 (79 kDa) penetrated far deeper into a sucrose density gradient than AXIN1 (96 kDa) in spite of its lower molecular weight, indicating that DVL2 forms protein complexes.
source: Performing ultracentrifugation assays, endogenous DVL2 (79 kDa) penetrated far deeper into a sucrose density gradient than AXIN1 (96 kDa) in spite of its lower molecular weight, indicating that DVL2 forms protein complexes (Figure 1A and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from ultracentrifugation assays shown in Figure 1A and E, demonstrating differential migration patterns of DVL2 and AXIN1.

claim: Most DVL2 molecules appeared to be engaged in protein complexes.
source: Noteworthy, most DVL2 molecules appeared to be engaged in these complexes (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A from ultracentrifugation assays.

claim: DVL2 complexes occurred in different cell lines.
source: The complexes occurred in different cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A demonstrating complexes in multiple cell lines.

claim: DVL2 complexes were detectable with two, siRNA-validated antibodies.
source: and were detectable with two, siRNA-validated antibodies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using two different antibodies validated by siRNA knockdown, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: DVL2 (79 kDa) showed a fractionation pattern similar to thyroglobulin (669 kDa), suggesting DVL2 complex sizes of about eight molecules assuming homotypic complexes.
source: DVL2 (79 kDa) showed a fractionation pattern similar to thyroglobulin (669 kDa), a commercial molecular weight marker, suggesting DVL2 complex sizes of about eight molecules assuming homotypic complexes (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data comparing DVL2 fractionation to a molecular weight marker (thyroglobulin) and inference about complex size from the molecular weight comparison.

claim: AXIN1 (96 kDa) showed a fractionation pattern similar to albumin (66 kDa) suggesting monomeric precipitation.
source: As a control, AXIN1 (96 kDa) showed a fractionation pattern similar to albumin (66 kDa) suggesting monomeric precipitation (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data comparing AXIN1 fractionation to a molecular weight marker (albumin) and inference about monomeric state.

claim: DVL2 complexes appeared to be paralog-specific because complexes were almost absent for DVL1 and DVL3.
source: Interestingly, the DVL2 complexes appeared to be paralog-specific because complexes were almost absent for DVL1 and DVL3 (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D comparing complex formation between DVL paralogs.

claim: The persistence of the complexes at low protein concentrations in cellular extracts indicated that they form via interaction sites with rather high affinity.
source: The persistence of the complexes at low protein concentrations in cellular extracts indicated that they form via interaction sites with rather high affinity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that complexes persist at low concentrations, which implies high-affinity interactions.

claim: The DIX domain is not involved in the formation of DVL2 complexes detected by ultracentrifugation.
source: Although the DIX domain is the best-characterized polymerization domain in DVL2 (Bienz, 2014), its low auto-affinity suggests that it is not involved in the formation of these complexes (Schwarz-Romond et al., 2007a).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from published literature about DIX domain affinity and citation to prior work.

claim: The striking difference between DVL2 and AXIN1 fractionation patterns pointed to the DIX domain not being involved in complex formation, since both proteins contain a functional DIX domain.
source: The striking difference between DVL2 and AXIN1 pointed in the same direction (Figure 1A), since both proteins contain a functional DIX domain (Kishida et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing DVL2 and AXIN1, combined with citation to prior work about DIX domains.

claim: A DIX domain-inhibiting point mutation (DVL2 M2) did not affect DVL2 complexes.
source: Consistently, a DIX domain-inhibiting point mutation (DVL2 M2) (Schwarz-Romond et al., 2007a) did not affect DVL2 complexes (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D, with reference to prior work characterizing the M2 mutation.

claim: Deletion of the DEP domain (construct ΔDEP) decreased DVL2 complexes.
source: Deletion of the DEP domain (construct ΔDEP) decreased DVL2 complexes, in line with its reported function in DVL2-DVL2 interaction (Gammons et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citation to prior work on DEP domain function.

claim: Additional deletion of residues 521–736 (construct 1–418) markedly reduced DVL2 complexes further compared to ΔDEP, demonstrating a strong contribution of the deleted residues to complex formation.
source: However, additional deletion of the remaining C-terminus (construct 1–418) markedly reduced them further, demonstrating a strong contribution of the deleted residues 521–736 to complex formation (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–C comparing different deletion constructs.

claim: Decreased protein complexation of DVL2 ΔDEP and 1–418 in ultracentrifugation experiments conspicuously correlated with decreased formation of condensates in immunofluorescence-based assays.
source: Importantly, decreased protein complexation of DVL2 ΔDEP and 1–418 in ultracentrifugation experiments conspicuously correlated with decreased formation of condensates in immunofluorescence-based assays (Figure 2D and E)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from two different assays shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Decreased protein complexation of DVL2 ΔDEP and 1–418 correlated with decreased Wnt pathway activation in reporter assays.
source: and decreased Wnt pathway activation in reporter assays (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from reporter assays shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The DVL2 complexes may be important for signaling activity.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that the DVL2 complexes may be important for signaling activity.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the correlation observed between complex formation and signaling activity.

claim: Four low-complexity regions (LCR1-4) were identified in DVL2 using the SEG algorithm.
source: We identified four low-complexity regions (LCR1-4), which are associated with protein assembly (Martin et al., 2020; Martin and Mittag, 2018)
evidence: The claim is based on computational prediction using the SEG algorithm and citation to prior work on low-complexity regions.

claim: One potential aggregation site was identified embedded in LCR4 using the TANGO algorithm.
source: one potential aggregation site embedded in LCR4
evidence: The claim is based on computational prediction using the TANGO algorithm.

claim: Two domains (CD1-2) whose evolutionary conservation may point to functional importance were identified.
source: and two domains whose evolutionary conservation may point to functional importance (CD1-2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is based on protein alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and inference about functional importance from conservation.

claim: Only deletion of LCR4 and CD2 decreased condensate formation and Wnt pathway activation of DVL2 ΔDEP upon individual deletion of the six identified regions LCR1-4 and CD1-2.
source: Upon individual deletion of the six identified regions LCR1-4 and CD1-2, only deletion of LCR4 and CD2 decreased condensate formation and Wnt pathway activation of DVL2 ΔDEP (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from deletion analysis shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Combined deletion of LCR4 and CD2 increased the effect on condensate formation and Wnt pathway activation compared to individual deletions.
source: Combined deletion of LCR4 and CD2 increased the effect (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: DVL2 ΔDEP-ΔCFR exhibited a marked decrease in the number of cells with condensates similar to 1–418.
source: DVL2 ΔDEP-ΔCFR exhibited a marked decrease in the number of cells with condensates (Figure 3A–C), in the number of condensates per cell (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–G) and in Wnt pathway activation (Figure 3E), similar to 1–418.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Individual or combined fusion of LCR4 and CD2 to 1–418 sufficed to induce condensation.
source: Importantly, individual or combined fusion of LCR4 and CD2 to 1–418 sufficed to induce condensation (Figure 3A–D; Figure 3—figure supplements 1D-G and Figure 3—figure supplements 2A and B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fusion constructs shown in multiple figures.

claim: Individual or combined fusion of LCR4 and CD2 to 1–418 sufficed to induce Wnt pathway activation.
source: and Wnt pathway activation (Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from reporter assays shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: Fusion of LCR4 and CD2 to 1–418 rendered 1–418+CFR as active as ΔDEP.
source: rendering 1–418+CFR as active as ΔDEP.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing activity levels of different constructs.

claim: Mutational inactivation of the DIX domain (1–418+CFR M2) abolished condensates demonstrating that the DIX domain is required for CFR-mediated condensates.
source: Mutational inactivation of the DIX domain (1–418+CFR M2) abolished condensates demonstrating that the DIX domain is required for CFR-mediated condensates (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mutant constructs shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The investigated DVL2 mutant proteins predominantly formed nuclear condensates in contrast to the cytosolic condensates of WT DVL2, most likely because a nuclear export signal was deleted in these mutants.
source: Interestingly, the investigated DVL2 mutant proteins predominantly formed nuclear condensates in contrast to the cytosolic condensates of WT DVL2, most likely, because a nuclear export signal (Figure 2A) was deleted in these mutants (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations shown in figures and inference about the mechanism involving nuclear export signal deletion.

claim: Investigating only cells with cytosolic condensates revealed similar differences between the DVL2 mutants as were observed when investigating mainly cells with nuclear condensates, suggesting that the detected differences are not due to nuclear localization but reflect the overall condensation capacity of the DVL2 mutants.
source: However, investigating only cells with cytosolic condensates (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and F) revealed similar differences between the DVL2 mutants as were observed when investigating mainly cells with nuclear condensates (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that the detected differences are not due to nuclear localization but reflect the overall condensation capacity of the DVL2 mutants.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data comparing nuclear and cytosolic condensates and inference about the mechanism.

claim: Fusion of CFR to the isolated DVL2 DIX or AXIN1 DAX domain sufficed to trigger condensation.
source: Moreover, fusion of CFR to the isolated DVL2 DIX or AXIN1 DAX domain sufficed to trigger condensation, which was prevented by M2/M3 mutation of the DIX/DAX domain (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D,G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fusion constructs shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D,G and H.

claim: M2/M3 mutation of the DIX/DAX domain prevented CFR-mediated condensation of DIX or DAX fusion constructs.
source: which was prevented by M2/M3 mutation of the DIX/DAX domain (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D,G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mutant constructs shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D,G and H.

claim: Loss- and gain-of-function experiments identified CFR as the crucial region for condensation and Wnt pathway activation within the DVL2 C-Terminus, which functionally cooperates with the DIX domain.
source: Thus, loss- and gain-of-function experiments identified CFR as the crucial region for condensation and Wnt pathway activation within the DVL2 C-Terminus, which functionally cooperates with the DIX domain.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results including deletion and fusion experiments.

claim: CFR deletion from ΔDEP (ΔDEP-ΔCFR) decreased DVL2 complexes detected by density gradient ultracentrifugation.
source: Indeed, CFR deletion from ΔDEP (ΔDEP-ΔCFR) and fusion with 1–418 (1–418+CFR) decreased and increased complexes, respectively (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from ultracentrifugation assays shown in Figure 4A–D.

claim: CFR fusion with 1–418 (1–418+CFR) increased DVL2 complexes detected by density gradient ultracentrifugation.
source: Indeed, CFR deletion from ΔDEP (ΔDEP-ΔCFR) and fusion with 1–418 (1–418+CFR) decreased and increased complexes, respectively (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from ultracentrifugation assays shown in Figure 4A–D.

claim: Replacing the respective sequence in DVL1 with the CFR of DVL2 (DVL1-CFRDVL2) promoted complex formation.
source: Moreover, replacing the respective sequence in DVL1 with the CFR of DVL2 (DVL1-CFRDVL2) promoted complex formation (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from chimeric constructs shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Only LCR4 but not CD2 was required for complex formation when deleted from ΔDEP.
source: Surprisingly, only LCR4 but not CD2 was required for complex formation when deleted from ΔDEP or mediated complex formation when fused to 1–418 (Figure 4A–D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from deletion and fusion constructs shown in Figure 4A–D.

claim: Only LCR4 but not CD2 mediated complex formation when fused to 1–418.
source: Surprisingly, only LCR4 but not CD2 was required for complex formation when deleted from ΔDEP or mediated complex formation when fused to 1–418 (Figure 4A–D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fusion constructs shown in Figure 4A–D.

claim: Both LCR4 and CD2 were required for condensate formation.
source: although both parts were required for condensate formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: LCR4 is not well conserved in DVL1 and DVL3, which do not form complexes.
source: Of note, LCR4 is not well conserved in DVL1 and DVL3, which do not form complexes (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and experimental data on complex formation shown in Figure 1C.

claim: DVL2 contains a bipartite, 58 amino acid region at the very C-Terminus consisting of a low complexity region (LCR4) that promotes complexes and condensates and a conserved domain (CD2) that only promotes condensates and is dispensable for complexes.
source: Together, our data revealed a bipartite, 58 amino acid region at the very C-Terminus of DVL2 consisting of a low complexity region (LCR4) that promotes complexes and condensates and a conserved domain (CD2) that only promotes condensates and is dispensable for complexes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results characterizing LCR4 and CD2 functions.

claim: LCR4 and CD2 might directly mediate DVL2-DVL2 interaction given their role in complex and condensate formation.
source: Given the role of the CFR parts LCR4 and CD2 in complex and condensate formation of DVL2, we speculated that they might directly mediate DVL2-DVL2 interaction.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed roles of LCR4 and CD2.

claim: LCR4 VV-AA mutation of DVL2 ΔDEP decreased condensate formation as efficiently as LCR4 deletion.
source: LCR4 VV-AA mutation of DVL2 ΔDEP decreased condensate formation as efficiently as LCR4 deletion (Figure 5B and C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing mutation and deletion effects shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Fusion of VV-AA-mutated LCR4 failed to increase condensate formation of 1–418, in contrast to WT LCR4.
source: and fusion of VV-AA-mutated LCR4 failed to increase condensate formation of 1–418, in contrast to WT LCR4 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fusion constructs shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: CD2 FF-AA mutation decreased condensate formation as efficiently as CD2 deletion.
source: CD2 FF-AA mutation decreased condensate formation and Wnt pathway activation as efficiently as CD2 deletion (Figure 5B and C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing mutation and deletion effects shown in Figure 5B and C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CD2 FF-AA mutation decreased Wnt pathway activation as efficiently as CD2 deletion.
source: CD2 FF-AA mutation decreased condensate formation and Wnt pathway activation as efficiently as CD2 deletion (Figure 5B and C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from reporter assays shown in Figure 5B and C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CD2 FF-AA fusion failed to increase condensate formation or Wnt pathway activation, in contrast to WT CD2.
source: and CD2 FF-AA fusion failed to increase condensate formation or Wnt pathway activation, in contrast to WT CD2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fusion constructs shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–G.

claim: CFR is a bipartite protein interaction site for self-association of DVL2.
source: Our data suggest that CFR is a bipartite protein interaction site for self-association of DVL2.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results characterizing CFR function.

claim: The isolated CFR accumulated within DVL2 condensates upon co-expression of both proteins.
source: In line with this, the isolated CFR, which exhibited a homogeneous cellular distribution when expressed alone, accumulated within DVL2 condensates upon co-expression of both proteins (Figure 5D and E), suggesting CFR-DVL2 interaction.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from co-expression experiments shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: CFR VV-AA FF-AA mutation markedly reduced CFR-DVL2 co-localization.
source: CFR VV-AA FF-AA mutation markedly reduced this CFR-DVL2 co-localization (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mutant constructs shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: DVL2 CFR did not co-localize with DVL1 or DVL3 condensates.
source: Moreover, DVL2 CFR did not co-localize with DVL1 or DVL3 condensates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H), consistent with the low conservation of the LCR4 aggregon in these paralogs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H and sequence conservation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Co-expression of the isolated CFR inhibited Wnt pathway activation by DVL2 in a dosage-dependent manner.
source: Notably, co-expression of the isolated CFR inhibited Wnt pathway activation by DVL2 in a dosage-dependent manner, which was attenuated by CFR FF-AA mutation (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from reporter assays shown in Figure 5F.

claim: CFR FF-AA mutation attenuated the inhibition of Wnt pathway activation by isolated CFR.
source: which was attenuated by CFR FF-AA mutation (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from reporter assays shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Free CFR might weaken DVL2-DVL2 interaction by saturating the interaction surface of the CFR within DVL2.
source: In this experiment, free CFR might weaken DVL2-DVL2 interaction by saturating the interaction surface of the CFR within DVL2.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism for the observed inhibition.

claim: CFR mediates intermolecular DVL2 self-interaction via an aggregation site in LCR4 and phenylalanine stickers in CD2.
source: Together, our data provide evidence that CFR mediates intermolecular DVL2 self-interaction via an aggregation site in LCR4 and phenylalanine stickers in CD2.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results characterizing LCR4 and CD2 interaction mechanisms.

claim: Both LCR4 and CD2 interaction sites most likely cooperate to drive the condensate formation of DVL2.
source: Since individual deletion of LCR4 or CD2 was sufficient to impair condensates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), both interaction sites most likely cooperate to drive the condensate formation of DVL2.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data on deletion effects shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 1–418 and DVL2 DIX exhibited a homogenous cellular distribution.
source: While 1–418 and DVL2 DIX exhibited a homogenous cellular distribution, fusion of CFR-induced spherical, microscopically visible condensates of 1–418+CFR and DIX+CFR (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Fusion of CFR induced spherical, microscopically visible condensates of 1–418+CFR and DIX+CFR.
source: fusion of CFR-induced spherical, microscopically visible condensates of 1–418+CFR and DIX+CFR (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Osmotic shock treatment significantly decreased condensates of DVL2, 1–418+CFR, and DIX+CFR within 3 min.
source: Both treatments significantly decreased condensates of all three studied proteins within 3 min for osmotic shock and 1 hr for 1,6-hexanediol (Figure 6A–C; Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from osmotic shock treatments shown in Figure 6A–C and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: 1,6-hexanediol treatment significantly decreased condensates of DVL2, 1–418+CFR, and DIX+CFR within 1 hr.
source: Both treatments significantly decreased condensates of all three studied proteins within 3 min for osmotic shock and 1 hr for 1,6-hexanediol (Figure 6A–C; Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 1,6-hexanediol treatments shown in Figure 6A–C and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: The findings from osmotic shock and 1,6-hexanediol treatments are consistent with the transition from a two-phase state of condensates to a one-phase state of homogenous protein distribution.
source: These findings are consistent with the transition from a two-phase state of condensates with high protein concentration and surrounding spaces with low protein concentration to a one-phase state of homogenous protein distribution (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations and established knowledge about phase separation.

claim: Fusion of an AXIN1-derived, sequence wise-nonrelated condensate-forming region (CFRAX) to DVL2 ΔDEP-ΔCFR (ΔDEP-ΔCFR+CFRAX) restored condensate formation to the level of ΔDEP.
source: Moreover, the fusion of an AXIN1-derived, sequence wise-nonrelated condensate-forming region (CFRAX, see Figure 6—figure supplement 1 for details) to DVL2 ΔDEP-ΔCFR (ΔDEP-ΔCFR+CFRAX) restored condensate formation to the level of ΔDEP (Figure 6D–F)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fusion constructs shown in Figure 6D–F.

claim: CFRAX fusion (ΔDEP-ΔCFR+CFRAX) rescued the decreased Wnt pathway activation of ΔDEP-ΔCFR compared to ΔDEP.
source: More importantly, CFRAX fusion (ΔDEP-ΔCFR+CFRAX) also rescued the decreased Wnt pathway activation of ΔDEP-ΔCFR compared to ΔDEP (Figure 6G)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from reporter assays shown in Figure 6G.

claim: It is the CFR phase-separating activity that is crucial for signaling.
source: suggesting that it is indeed the CFR phase-separating activity that is crucial for signaling.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the rescue experiment with CFRAX.

claim: The oligomeric complexes detected by ultracentrifugation showed sizes of about eight DVL2 molecules, which were irrespective of expression levels as they were similar between endogenous and overexpressed DVL2.
source: The complexes detected by ultracentrifugation showed sizes of about eight DVL2 molecules, which were irrespective of expression levels as they were similar between endogenous and overexpressed DVL2 (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing endogenous and overexpressed DVL2 shown in Figure 1A–C.

claim: The oligomeric complexes cannot be identical with the known microscopically visible condensates, containing thousands of molecules.
source: Therefore, the complexes cannot be identical with the known microscopically visible condensates, containing thousands of molecules.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the size difference between complexes and condensates.

claim: The oligomeric complexes existed in parallel to the condensates or constituted a condensate substructure.
source: These oligomeric complexes thus existed in parallel to the condensates or constituted a condensate substructure.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing possible relationships between complexes and condensates.

claim: DVL2 contains domains that promote both complexes and condensates, such as LCR4 and DEP.
source: Analysis of mutant DVL2 proteins revealed that DVL2 contains domains that promote both complexes and condensates, such as LCR4 and DEP (Figure 2B–E; Figure 4A-D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data analyzing different DVL2 domains shown in multiple figures.

claim: DVL2 contains domains that promote only condensates but not complexes, such as CD2 and DIX.
source: and domains that promote only condensates but not complexes, such as CD2 and DIX (Figure 1C; Figure 4A–D; Figure 7C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data analyzing different DVL2 domains shown in multiple figures.

claim: All DVL2 mutations that reduced complexes also affected condensates.
source: However, all DVL2 mutations that reduced complexes also affected condensates.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experimental results with different mutations.

claim: The oligomeric complexes are required for and possibly represent substructures of the multimeric condensates.
source: Therefore, we suggest that the oligomeric complexes are required for and possibly represent substructures of the multimeric condensates (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the correlation between complex and condensate formation and is illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: Complex formation via LCR4 and DEP precedes further assembly of these substructures into condensates via CD2 and DIX.
source: As the stability of complexes at low protein concentrations, e.g., in cellular extracts, indicated a rather high affinity of the underlying interaction sites (Figure 1A), we hypothesize that complex formation via LCR4 and DEP precedes further assembly of these substructures into condensates via CD2 and DIX (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a two-step model based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: The proposed two-step model of DVL2 condensate formation is in line with and supportive of the emerging stickers model for the formation of biomolecular condensates.
source: Our proposed two-step model of DVL2 condensate formation is in line with and supportive of the emerging stickers model for the formation of biomolecular condensates (Choi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on inference connecting the experimental findings to an established theoretical model, with citation to prior work.

claim: According to the stickers model, oligomerization via one interaction site can drive subsequent condensate formation by increasing the valence of another interaction site (=sticker) of the oligomer compared to a monomer.
source: According to this model, oligomerization via one interaction site can drive subsequent condensate formation by increasing the valence of another interaction site (=sticker) of the oligomer compared to a monomer (Choi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on citation to prior work describing the stickers model.

claim: The proposed two-step model would increase the options for regulating the polymerization of DVL2 by modulating the oligomerization step or the condensate formation step.
source: The proposed two-step model would increase the options for regulating the polymerization of DVL2 by modulating the oligomerization step or the condensate formation step (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing implications of the two-step model for regulation.

claim: DVL2 polymerization is crucial for Wnt signal transduction.
source: DVL2 polymerization is crucial for Wnt signal transduction.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Pre-oligomerization of DVL2 via high-affinity interactions as identified in the ultracentrifugation assay might facilitate Wnt-induced polymerization.
source: Pre-oligomerization of DVL2 via high-affinity interactions as identified in the ultracentrifugation assay might facilitate Wnt-induced polymerization.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: The discovered C-terminal self-interaction site CFR may contribute to the regulation of DVL2 condensates through conformational changes.
source: Furthermore, the discovered C-terminal self-interaction site CFR may contribute to the regulation of DVL2 condensates through conformational changes.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a regulatory mechanism.

claim: Binding of the very C-terminus of DVL2 to its PDZ domain results in a closed protein conformation.
source: Binding of the very C-terminus of DVL2 to its PDZ domain results in a closed protein conformation (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on citation to prior work.

claim: The closed conformation limits the accessibility of the N-terminal intrinsically disordered region that promotes condensate formation, thereby suppressing DVL2 condensates.
source: It has been suggested that this closed conformation limits the accessibility of the N-terminal intrinsically disordered region that promotes condensate formation, thereby suppressing DVL2 condensates (Kang et al., 2022; Vamadevan et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is based on citation to prior work.

claim: Condensate formation will be additionally suppressed in the closed conformation by limiting the accessibility of CFR because only one amino acid separates the identified crucial phenylalanine residues of CFR from the PDZ binding motif in the DVL2 C-terminus.
source: It is very intriguing to speculate that condensate formation will be additionally suppressed in the closed conformation by limiting the accessibility of CFR because only one amino acid separates the identified crucial phenylalanine residues of CFR from the PDZ binding motif in the DVL2 C-terminus.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism based on structural considerations.

claim: Wnt ligands induce the open DVL conformation.
source: Notably, Wnt ligands induce the open DVL conformation (Harnoš et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is based on citation to prior work.

claim: The open DVL conformation will increase the CFR accessibility and allow LCR4 and CD2 to contribute to pre-oligomerization and subsequent condensate formation of DVL2, respectively.
source: which will increase the CFR accessibility and, according to our model, would allow LCR4 and CD2 to contribute to pre-oligomerization and subsequent condensate formation of DVL2, respectively.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism based on the model and prior work on conformational changes.

claim: Several studies suggest functional differences between the DVL paralogs.
source: Several studies suggest functional differences between the DVL paralogs (Gentzel et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2008; Paclíková et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is based on citation to multiple prior studies.

claim: Complex formation as revealed by ultracentrifugation was only observed for DVL2 and not for DVL1 or DVL3, revealing a marked difference between the paralogs.
source: Notably, complex formation as revealed by ultracentrifugation was only observed for DVL2 and not for DVL1 or DVL3, revealing a marked difference between the paralogs (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CFR did not co-localize with DVL1 or DVL3 in contrast to DVL2, indicating that CFR-mediated DVL2-DVL2 interaction is absent from DVL1 and DVL3.
source: In addition, CFR did not co-localize with DVL1 or DVL3 in contrast to DVL2, indicating that CFR-mediated DVL2-DVL2 interaction, which most likely drove DVL2 complexation, is absent from DVL1 and DVL3 (Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1H and inference about the mechanism.
